tittel: Obasanjo on population and development.
sammendrag: At the Farm House Dialogue meeting in Nigeria in 2001 good health was defined as a state of physical psychological and social well-being which enables an individual to lead an optimally productive life. Participants observed that women children and the aged are the most vulnerable group in the society in matters of health care. It was also recognized that the prevailing poor health status of most women was a reflection of their low societal status and the general problem of poverty in the society. In addition women suffer from cultural taboos and practices such as female circumcision mishandling of umbilical cord during delivery poor methods of child weaning and several nutritional taboos. Lack of education on simple hygiene and preventive health care as well as the activities of uneducated traditional birth attendants also compound the problems of pregnancy labor and birth. In this perspective the Dialogue suggested that clinics should be established in rural and urban centers to facilitate primary health care delivery provide adequate maternal and child care and make essential drugs readily available and accessible. Lastly it was stressed that greater emphasis should be placed on creating awareness among women to increase usage of these facilities.

tittel: Bach returns to Cambridge
sammendrag: After a two-year pandemic pause, the Bach Network hosted its tenth Dialogue Meeting at Madingley Hall in the beautiful Cambridgeshire countryside. The meeting began on Monday 18 July 2023 with a short harpsichord recital by Dan Tidhar and Joel Speerstra who had the distinction of performing during the warmest hour in the warmest place on the warmest day in Britain’s recorded history. The week-long conference, enjoying steadily cooler weather, followed a now well-established Bach Network pattern where multiple platforms for presentation create meaningful dialogue and lively discussion. With no parallel sessions, everyone was able to listen to and discuss over 50 presentations. In five-minute flash sessions we heard updates about new work from around the globe. In informal evening interviews, Steven Isserlis discussed his new book on the Bach cello suites with John Butt, and Michael Marissen interviewed Michael Maul who took us behind the scenes at the Leipzig Bach Festival, discussing recent events (including correspondence with Pope Benedict) and future plans from his perspective as Festival Director.

tittel: Developing a Christian Character Education Class through Work-oriented Education and Circle Dialogue
sammendrag: Social Distancing due to COVID-19 limits the basic human needs of creation, relationships, and communication. Education in the post-COVID era should thus be about restoring the value of relationships and cooperation. Work activities and circle dialogues are part of this. Students may realize the principle of forming a good mind by understanding the principle of life, the cycle of nature, and the distribution of resources through work(like farming and woodworking). Students may secure a safe space by living together, holding regular circle dialogue meetings in class, sharing their thoughts, and listening to others" opinions. The purpose of this study is to develop and verify the effectiveness of character class for the cultivation of a field of the heart and sense of community, which form the basis of character competency for middle school students in the COVID-19 era. Students are able to experience the value of labor and lay the foundation for coexistence through activities related to farming and woodworking, production and sharing. In this process, circle gatherings act as a small ecosystem where students experience living together in a mutually equal relationship. After developing the model of a character education class centered on work and circle dialogue, we explore the effect of the class through observation and in-depth interviews.

tittel: An Audit of the Management of Neonatal Jaundice in a Level 2 Neonatology Unit of a Maternity Hospital Against the 2023 NICE Guidelines
sammendrag: BackgroundIn Pakistan, neonatal jaundice is a common cause of neonatal morbidity.This audit was conducted to evaluate adherence by the local team to NICE (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence) guidelines in the management of neonatal jaundice in children under 28 days of life admitted to the Level 2 Neonatology Unit of Maternity Hospital and to identify any deviations from NICE guidelines regarding the assessment, monitoring, and treatment to improve care provided to neonates with jaundice. MethodsAround 46 neonates admitted and diagnosed with visually apparent jaundice or at risk of jaundice at the Neonatal Unit of Maternity Hospital were included from February 2024 to April 2024.We included data on history, clinical examination, serum total bilirubin measurements, and jaundice management and analyzed them using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 26 (Released 2018; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). ResultsWe included 46 neonates with a mean age of 3.17 ± 1.371 days, gestational age of 35.07 ± 2.768 weeks, and mean weight of 2.17 ± 0.677 kg.Visual jaundice was present in 91.3% (N = 42/46), but only 21.7% (N = 10/46) had serum bilirubin levels requiring phototherapy, with a p-value of 0.27.Interventions were proactive: 21.7% (N = 10/46) received phototherapy, and 52.2% (N = 24/46) had bilirubin monitoring.Risk factor documentation and follow-up plans were high: 87% (N = 40/46) and 84.8% (N = 39/46), respectively.Patient education was thorough, at 93.5% (N = 43/46).There was 54.3% (N = 25/46) adherence to NICE guidelines regarding serum bilirubin levels, need for phototherapy, bilirubin monitoring frequency, patient education, and follow-up plans in the local setup, compared with the 100% (N = 46/46) standard, emphasizing the need for improvement. ConclusionWhile the audit indicates satisfactory levels of guideline adherence in certain areas of neonatal jaundice management, it also highlights significant areas for improvement, which are crucial for optimizing care outcomes in the management of jaundice in neonates.

tittel: What breast cancer survivors can teach us about the labor market
kilde: Research at the University of Copenhagen (University of Copenhagen)
sammendrag: In this op-ed, the author draws on her own experience of breast cancer and four years of anthropological research, including participation in support groups run by the Danish Cancer Society and interviews with women treated for breast cancer, to ask why so many struggle to return to work after treatment. More than half of the women who resume full-time work after chemotherapy go on to develop stress, and many change jobs or move to part-time. Danish cancer policy, most recently Cancer Plan 5 with its regional clinics for late effects, responds by treating individual symptoms, while the path back to work depends on how municipalities, caseworkers, employers, and managers happen to carry out each person’s follow-up plan. Several women described their treatment as a welcome pause that led them to reconsider how much space work should occupy in their lives. That personal reorientation collides with workplaces whose pace and workload remain unchanged. The article argues that the sick leave, job changes, and shifts to part-time among cancer survivors act as a canary in the coal mine, signaling that the pursuit of efficiency has produced a labor market few can sustain. Instead of increasing pressure on those who choose to work less, policymakers should listen to those who want to work differently: fewer simultaneous tasks, flexible hours, and less pressure on productivity.

tittel: Staff planning optimisation : Company X
sammendrag:
The purpose of this research was to find out how the staff planning at Company X is perceived and how it could be further improved in the sales function. The objective was to find new staff planning strategies and to do a case study on one of the store's departments. With the case study department, a new rota was planned together with the department and a follow-up planned. Parts of this thesis are bound to secrecy and are not published. 
 
The data for this thesis was collected using both quantitative and qualitative data collection methods. Surveys and open discussion were used with the case study department of 10 people. A total of 11 people were interviewed for the general part of this research. The interviews were semi-structured interviews. There was no ready-made set of questions, but rather a framework of themes discussed with the interviewees. 
 
The major findings of this research were that the duty rosters should be available in an electronic format as well as the forms related to it, such as day off wishes and shift switches. It was also found out that the competence of the co-workers should be developed in order to being able to back up sick leaves and help with sudden queues. All managers should also go through their department's rota with the co-workers for hour allocation optimisation. 
 
This thesis provides the starting point for staff planning optimisation at Company X. The results will be discussed and analyzed together with the store's management group and all the managers in sales, and an action plan will be made. It would be interesting and recommended to conduct a similar research for other functions, too. This thesis can be used as a basis for similar researches at different companies in the future.

tittel: Penguatan IRAMA (Insan Ramah Aktif Menarik Dan Aktual) Melalui Pelatihan Entrepreneurship Berbasis Pendidikan Abad 21
sammendrag: This article contains the results of the Community Partnership Program (PKM) Activities carried out in Rancakole Village, Arjasari District, Bandung Regency, West Java. This activity was motivated based on observations made by the PKM team, that in this village most of the residents work as sellers of curtains. However, currently its sales assets are decreasing due to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. So that when the team conducted the field survey, many people complained about this situation, and it has impact for residents in the village to become sick as the result of psychological and economic stress problems. Therefore, the UHAMKA Community Partnership Program (PKM) team offered a solution by strengthening these residents in various aspects, including communication, creativity, performance, and knowledge. One form of its activities is by holding 21st Century Education-Based Entrepreneurship Training which aims to provide reinforcement for Individuals to be more Friendly, Active, Attractive, and Actual which is abbreviated in Bahasa as IRAMA. In this activity, the residents were given training that focuses on communication techniques in sales so that they can adjust to current conditions. In this training, the resource persons trained on basic communication techniques in sales, how to read market opportunities through a SWOT analysis, and how the role of parents for children during the COVID-19 pandemic. As the results, the participants made Follow-up Plan related to how to do entrepreneurship by using a SWOT analysis and by applying the right communication techniques so that they become productive people during the COVID-19 pandemic.

tittel: The impact that a Post Acute kidney injury clinic can have on a patient's journey.
sammendrag: Introduction AKI poses a worldwide concern, with a notable prevalence among patients in various acute care settings (NICE, 2023, NICE, 2021a). This condition is linked to substantial clinical repercussions and increased healthcare expenditures, attributing cost of over 1 billion pound in the UK (Kerr, Bedford, Matthews & Donoghue, 2014). Studies have indicated that preventive measures and prompt AKI identification can enhance outcomes. Ensuring excellent care for patients with AKI by recognising at community level and extending through the emergency department , hospital environment, and post-discharge from inpatient care (Renal Association, 2019). Materials & method We invited all eligible patients who had been identified as experiencing AKI, dedicating a half-hour clinic appointment to their care where we delved into the patients' journey throughout their admission, discussing the AKI diagnosis, risk factors, management, and recovery. These clinics served as opportunities to provide patient education, offer health advice, medication review and formulate plans for ongoing management. Throughout the process, we gathered data, incorporating patient feedback and outcomes. Results & discussion Over a quarter of the patients in the clinic did not know that they had an AKI during their inpatient stay. Additionally, 70% reported they knew little or nothing about AKI and what it meant prior to their clinic appointment. The Post AKI clinic, addresses gaps in primary care and significantly contributing to the delivery of patient education surrounding medicine management , sick day guidance and providing healthy kidney advice (NICE 2021a). This service also contributes to enhanced patient journey. The feedback from the patient survey showed that the Post AKI clinic helped 87.6% understand more about AKI and of that, 46% of those patients learnt it from a nurse and 38.5% learnt it from a doctor. Around 85% felt the clinic helped them to understand their individual risk factors with 84.5% having a clear understanding of medicine management and sick day guidance in the future to reduce risk of a reoccurring AKI NICE guidance recognised that adults discharged from hospital post AKI are at higher risk of ongoing health issues but follow up enables early identification, prevention and this reduce readmission (NICE, 2023). The trust readmission rate, since the Post AKI clinic was introduced, has gone from an average of 17% to now 14.8%. The average inpatient length of stay was 20 days and has reduced to 16.8 days highlighting another positive outcome from Post AKI clinics. Conclusion The data illustrates enhanced patient satisfaction and experience. This directly benefits patients and aligns with the aims outlined in the NICE guidance for early detection and prevention (NICE, 2021a). Moreover, the Post AKI clinic has proven its effectiveness in reducing hospital readmissions and it contributes to a reduced length of hospital stay by instilling confidence in care teams for early discharge, accompanied by a comprehensive follow-up plan. In summary, the Post AKI clinic has proven to be a success for both patients and the hospital.

tittel: Knowledge on Hospital Discharge Information Among Patients With Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy at a Tertiary Hospital in Tanzania
sammendrag: Abstract Background: Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy (HDP) are one of the leading causes of the persistently high maternal mortality ratio in Tanzania. Complications of HDP can occur during pregnancy, delivery or postpartum period hence prevention of these partly depends on the patient’s understanding of information given during discharge from hospitals. The aim of this study was to assess the knowledge of vital information given to patients at the time of discharge. Methods: A cross-sectional study was carried out at Muhimbili National Hospital in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania from September to November 2020. Exit face-to-face interviews were conducted among 422 women treated for HDP who were conveniently recruited at the time of discharge. A Swahili translated structured questionnaire adapted from World Health Organization (WHO), California Medical Quality Care Collaborative tool kit (CMQCC) and previous studies was used to collect data. The questionnaire consisted of 4 domains; knowledge on postpartum danger signs, diagnosis, medication, and follow-up plan. A score of at least half or more of the maximum score in each domain were defined as adequate knowledge. Data collected was analyzed using Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS) version 23.0. Descriptive statistics, chi-square test and logistic regression was used to determine factors that strongly affect the knowledge on discharge information. The results were expressed as Odds Ratio (OR), with statistically significant level at p<0.05. Results: Seventy-three percent of women with HDP had adequate knowledge on the hospital discharge information. Furthermore, 79% of women had adequate knowledge on postpartum danger signs, 77% in diagnosis, 87% in prescribed medications and 92% in follow up plan. Women who were married, employed, with higher level of education, booked ANC at an early gestational age of less than four months and had more than four ANC visits were more likely to have adequate knowledge on hospital discharge information. Conclusion: Most women with HDP had an adequate knowledge on their discharge information. As observed from our study, most women were in the younger age group and primiparous. Greater emphasis and a more tailored education should be given to these women due to high rate of recurrence of HDP in subsequent pregnancies.

tittel: POLICY OF HEALTH CHECK-UP ON PROSPECTIVE HAJJ PILGRIMS
sammendrag: The purpose of this study is to investigate and analyze the health examination policy for Prospective Hajj Pilgrims (PHP) and the issues encountered. The research method employed is juridical-normative, using a legislative approach, with secondary data consisting of legislation and reference sources. The collected data were analyzed using descriptive-analytical techniques. The findings indicate that the PHP health examination program by the district health office has implemented the Minister of Health Regulation regarding PHP Health Isthita'ah through a first and second stage examination mechanism for determining health isthita'ah status which includes anamnesis, physical examination, supporting examinations, diagnosis, determination of health isthita'ah, recommendations, and follow-up plans on examination results. However, there are policy gaps regulating disease criteria that meet the istitaah requirements and are fit to fly at the third stage of inspection. There is no continuity of the first and second stage inspection policy with airworthiness. Technical instructions that regulate the limits of the health development program for PHP need to be adjusted to improve the health status of those PHP and provide certainty regarding the departure of PHP in terms of health.

tittel: Implementation of Discharge Planning using Leaflet Media for Coronary Heart Disease Patients in Indonesian Hospital
kilde: Journal of Health Medicine and Nursing
sammendrag: Coronary Heart Disease is one of the leading causes of illness and death worldwide. Patients with coronary heart disease often experience recurring events and require effective discharge planning to ensure continuity of care and prevent further complications. Proper discharge planning can enhance patients' understanding of their condition management and reduce the likelihood of rehospitalization. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of discharge planning in improving patient adherence to treatment and enhancing quality of life to reduce readmission rates among patients with Coronary Heart Disease (CHD). The research method employed is a descriptive case study. The study sample consists of CHD patients hospitalized in a hospital setting. During their hospital stay, patients received structured discharge planning, including health education, follow-up plans, and coordination with healthcare services. The results of implementing the discharge planning intervention over 3 days showed differences in knowledge levels before and after the intervention. Following education, improvements were observed in patients' knowledge regarding implementing care programs, taking actions to mitigate risks, and engaging in daily activities to achieve health goals.

tittel: Experimental Studies on Relapse of Full-Term Neonatal Jaundice after Phototherapy
kilde: Biomedical Journal of Scientific & Technical Research
sammendrag: Objective: Learn about the status of laboratory testing relapse after neonatal jaundice phototherapy.Methods: Sample of phototherapy full-term neonatal children with high blood bilirubin 222 cases, divided into 2 groups, according to the treatment result Relapse Group After phototherapy (31 cases), and NO Relapse Group After phototherapy (191 cases).Observing key laboratory test index of two groups such as G6PD, blood, blood routine, liver meritorious service etc.Results: Before Phototherapy, the Hb of Relapse Group After Phototherapy (149.63±14.71)g/l is obviously lower than these (156.02±17.90)g/l of NO Relapse After Phototherapy Group, t=2.169,P=0.035.After Phototherapy, the incidence of ABO hemolytic disease of newborn of Relapse Group is (16.13%)significantly higher than those(4.71%) of NO Relapse Grou , t = 5.857, P = 0.016;And the difference between other indicators of the two groups of neonate has no statistical significance (P < 0.050).Those indicators are AFP, ALT, AST, TBIL, HCT, MCHC and G6PD.Conclusion: Relapse of full-term neonatal jaundice after phototherapy may be related to lower hemoglobin concentration and ABO hemolytic disease.In order to improve curative effect, these risk factors should be taken into consideration when making Follow-up plan after phototherapy.

tittel: Treatment and rehabilitation of attempted suicide patients : an exploratory study of 71 cases admitted to Vancouver General Hospital in 1948
sammendrag: This is an exploratory assessment of the help given suicide patients admitted to a general hospital. The focus of the study is twofold: (a) to examine the kind of treatment administered at the hospital, including rehabilitation and follow-up plans for each patient; and (b) to determine the role of the social worker in this program. The study is based on the examination of the hospital records of 71 patients, who attempted suicide in 1948, and were admitted to Vancouver General Hospital for observation and treatment. The group as a whole is described with the aid of statistical data, no attempt being made to deduce causes from this evidence. More emphasis has been placed on the mental and emotional aspects of suicide, to outline some of the deeper, unconscious causations of suicidal behaviour. Case illustrations are discussed in the attempt to exemplify these factors. The theoretical background of the thesis is drawn from psychiatric literature in United States and Great Britain. Evidence in this study suggest that almost no help is given these patients, in the hospital, to relieve the psychological and social conflicts. There are grounds for urging that the social worker could play a valuable role in the treatment team, and that social work services are not being used to the extent they could be. Suggestions are presented regarding an adequate hospital program for suicidal patients, in which the psychiatrists, social worker, psychologist and nurses would work together to make a clinical study of each patient. On the basis of adequate clinical study, constructive recommendations on treatment and rehabilitation plans could be made, and the groundwork laid for an adequate program of follow-up services.

tittel: A Service Evaluation on How Mental Health of Learning Disability (MHLD) Services Across Kent Respond to Dementia Referrals
sammendrag: Aims: People with intellectual disability have a higher risk of developing dementia, yet assessment and diagnostic pathways can vary across services and regions. This service evaluation aims to evaluate how dementia referrals for people with intellectual disability are processed within Mental Health of Learning Disability (MHLD) services across Kent and identify opportunities to standardise referral and care pathways. Methods: A retrospective review was conducted of all referrals received by MHLD services in Kent from June 2022 to May 2023. Referrals were included if they contained themes suggestive of cognitive decline: changes in memory or function, forgetfulness, and confusion. Data were collected on referral source, demographics, reason for referral, acceptance or refusal, assessing discipline, follow-up plans, diagnoses at initial assessment and at 3 months. Referrals were analysed by region. Results: A total of 47 referrals met inclusion criteria. Acceptance rates varied by region and accepted referrals were younger on average than refused referrals across all regions. Down’s syndrome was present in a substantial proportion of accepted cases. Regional variation was observed in diagnostic pathways. Initiation of medication for dementia varied by clinician with consultants more likely to commence treatment than trainees. Conclusion: This evaluation highlighted regional variation in diagnostic pathways for people with intellectual disability and suspected dementia. The variation suggests a need for a standardised dementia referral and diagnostic pathway, guidance on in-house diagnosis, enhanced training for clinicians and allocation of wider resources to improve equity, efficiency and quality of care.

tittel: Living with breast cancer: policy practices and recommendations
sammendrag: The main aim of this thesis is to understand experiences, troubles and needs of women with breast cancer and caregivers. It will also attempt to make evidence-based health and social policy recommendations in order to enhance their quality of life and care. For these ends, current cancer related health and social policies of different countries and Turkey are reviewed and these countries are classified into four groups according to their scores in Human Development index. Also, semi structured in-depth interviews are conducted with 16 women with breast cancer, 7 caregivers from family members and 4 experts in Ankara and Izmir. This study reveals that there are physical, psychological, economic and familial impacts of breast cancer on patients and caregivers. Also, there are several institutional deficiencies which adversely influence the quality of life and care of women with breast cancer and caregivers. Based on findings of the field study and review of ongoing cancer policies from different countries, this thesis recommends evidence-based health and social policy regulations. These recommendations are as follows: introduction of personalized treatment, a regular assistance for housework and cooking, nationwide transportation system, legal arrangements regulating working lives of patients and caregivers, continuous psycho-oncological support and follow-up plans, regular familial therapies, a compulsory training program to develop communication skills of oncology professionals, elimination of inequalities among hospitals, cities and regions in terms of infrastructure and human resources, development of new informative channels, establishment of a national database about the treatment process and an international database including social policy regulations about cancer and also increase the role of social workers in breast cancer treatment process.

tittel: Scanning tiny minds: Cranial ultrasound findings in preterm neonates in special newborn care unit/neonatal intensive care unit
sammendrag: Background: Preterm birth remains a major global health concern and is a leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality. Cranial ultrasound (USG), being a safe, non-invasive, and bedside-available imaging tool, is widely used for screening and monitoring brain abnormalities in preterm infants. In tertiary care settings, where high-risk neonates are managed, understanding the spectrum of cranial USG findings can guide clinicians in decision-making and follow-up planning. Aims and Objectives: This study aims to assess the different clinical presentations of neonates with abnormal cranial USG. Materials and Methods: The observational descriptive study was conducted in the special newborn care unit/neonatal intensive care unit (SNCU/NICU) of Malda Medical College and Hospital for the period of 1 year. Preterm neonates admitted to SNCU/NICU were included. The first consecutive 100 preterm newborns admitted during the study period in SNCU/NICU from 15 December 2022 to 14 December 2023 were taken. Results: In this study, the majority of the cases were males (68%), and 17% of the cases, parents were married within 18 years. For most (60%) of the cases, gestational age was ≤32 weeks. Regarding cranial USG findings, abnormality was seen in 21% of cases. The gestational age and birth weight had a significant association with cranial USG findings. Conclusion: Cranial USG helps in early identification of neurological abnormalities among preterm as well as term neonates because of its high efficiency. Early identification of such abnormalities will help to prevent, protect, and further manage adversely affected infants. The same was observed in this study.

tittel: Improving continuity of care in urgent care
sammendrag: Introduction: Urgent care clinics are quick, convenient, and fit easily into the busy lifestyles of Americans. After an urgent care encounter, a patient's medical management and follow-up care with their primary care provider becomes inconsistent. This is especially problematic for adults 65 and older and individuals with chronic co-morbid conditions. The use of innovative technology, such as the electronic medical records and online patient portals, are proven to improve workflows and facilitate continual patient care. An urgent care clinic, founded by a healthcare system in southern New Jersey, established a need to improve patient follow-up care after an urgent care encounter. Method: Using the Plan-Do-Check-Act refinement methodology, this quality improvement project implemented a change in the current workflow to include a check-in and check-out process. The redesigned workflow incorporated innovative online technology, which quantitatively demonstrated an increase follow-up and continuity of care. Results: Through quantitative statistical analysis, each enrolled participant had either a new or established primary care provider and a definitive follow-up plan. Each participant had an online patient portal link sent via SMS or email. The McNemar test determined a statistically significant increase in follow-up based on the recommendation of the urgent care provider ([chi]2(1) = 52.019, p < .001). Conclusion: The improved workflow provided each participant the tools to stay engaged with their PCP and to close the gap of inconsistent care. Health information technology, in the way of electronic medical records (EMRs) and online patient portals, are essential to increase and improve continual health management.

tittel: Knowledge and Attitude Towards Anti-Retroviral Therapy Adherence among HIV/AIDS patients at Consolata Hospital Nkubu, Meru County, Kenya.
sammendrag: Poor adherence to the management of HIV/AIDS continues to pose a challenge in sub-Saharan Africa. To achieve the 90:90:90 target by the year 2020, optimum suppression of HIV requires a high level of adherence to prescribed treatment, counselling and follow-up plans. The number of people living with HIV in Meru County is estimated to be 20700 but only14205 are on Anti-Retroviral Therapy (ART) with a viral suppression rate of 69%. There is still scarcity of information on factors influencing adherence in Meru County and more so at Consolata Hospital. The study aimed at assessing knowledge and attitude towards anti-retroviral therapy adherence among HIV/AIDs patients at Consolata Hospital Nkubu. A descriptive cross sectional research design was adopted and 312 participants attending Comprehensive Care Clinic selected using systematic random sampling technique. Qualitative and quantitative data was collected using structured questionnaire. It was then cleaned, coded and entered into statistical package for social science (SPSS) version 23. Analysis was then done using both descriptive and inferential statistics and presented in tables and charts. The results showed that the majority of the respondents 108 (34.6%) were aged between 39-48 years and those with college education were (45.2%). The level of education was found to have a slight but statistically significant effect on ART adherence (p=0.04). Males were found to be 5 times more likely to miss drugs than females (OR= 5.23, X² =16.14, p<0.001). There was a statistically significant positive relationship between knowledge of ART and adherence (R=.81, p<0.001). This indicates that adherence is dependent on knowledge on ART. A statistically significant positive relationship between attitude and adherence was found (R=.66, p<0.001). Privacy and confidentiality was also shown to influence adherence to ART. The study recommends use of innovative approaches to improve on knowledge and follow up of clients.

tittel: Pemberdayaan kader kesehatan dalam meningkatkan kemampuan melakukan assessment dukungan keluarga pada lansia dengan penyakit kronis
sammendrag: Abstrak Desa Gunungronggo merupakan salah satu desa binaan Program Studi Sarjana Keperawatan yang berada di kecamatan Tajinan Kabupaten Malang. Jumlah lansia yang menderita penyakit kronis di Desa Gunungronggo cukup banyak yaitu 135 lansia. Berdasarkan buku kunjungan posyandu, belum semua lansia yang menderita penyakit kronis datang kontrol secara rutin salah satu alasannya karena tidak ada keluarga yang mengantar. Keluarga menyampaikan alasan tidak mengantar karena sibuk bekerja dan lansia sudah tidak ada keluhan sehingga keluarga menganggap tidak perlu lagi untuk memeriksakan diri atau kontrol. Salah satu peran keluarga dalam perawatan lansia yang sakit adalah memberikan motivasi, dukungan dan memfasilitasi kebutuhan kesehatan bagi lansia. Pada kegiatan ini tim pengabdian masyarakat melakukan pemberdayaan kader kesehatan dengan memberikan edukasi dan pelatihan bagi kader kesehatan dalam melakukan assesment dukungan keluarga pada lansia dengan penyakit kronis. Hasil pengukuran pre dan post test didapatkan bahwa pada tahap pre test rata-rata pengetahuan kader kesehatan adalah 62,73 sedangkan pada tahap post test didapatkan rata-rata pengetahuan meningkat menjadi 77,27 setelah diberikan materi dan pelatihan. Hasil evaluasi untuk ketrampilan kader kesehatan mampu melakukan dengan baik 100% semua tindakan sesuai prosedur. Peserta memberikan respon dan sangat antusias terhadap materi. Oleh karena itu perlu ditingkatkan kegiatan edukasi dan pelatihan kepada kader kesehatan, maka rekomendasi rencana tindak lanjut yang diajukan oleh tim adalah kegiatan serupa dilaksanakan secara kontinu sehingga adanya peningkatan kemandirian masyarakat dalam melakukan assesment dukungan keluarga pada lansia dengan penyakit kronis sehingga dapat meningkatkan kualitas hidup lansia khususnya yang menderita penyakit kronis. Kata kunci: pemberdayaan kader; assessment; dukungan keluarga lansia; penyakit kronis. Abstract Gunungronggo Village is one of the villages supported by the Bachelor of Nursing Study Program in Tajinan sub-district, Malang Regency. Number of elderly people suffering from chronic diseases In Gunungronggo Village there are quite a lot, namely 135 elderly people. Based on the posyandu visit book, not all elderly people who suffer from chronic diseases come for routine check-ups, one of the reasons is because there is no family to accompany them. The family stated that the reason for not taking them was because they were busy working and the elderly had no complaints, so the family thought there was no need for further examination or control. One of the roles of the family in caring for sick elderly people is to provide motivation, support and facilitate the health needs of the elderly. In this activity, the community service team empowered health cadres by providing education and training for health cadres in conducting family support assessments for elderly people with chronic diseases. The results of the pre and post test measurements showed that at the pre test stage the average knowledge of health cadres was 62.73, while at the post test stage it was found that the average knowledge increased, namely 77.27 after being given material and training. The evaluation results for the skills of health cadres are able to carry out 100% of all actions according to procedures. Participants responded and were very enthusiastic about the material. Therefore,it is necessary to increase education and training activities for health cadres, so the recommendation for the follow-up plan proposed by the team is that similar activities be carried out continuously so that there is increased community independence in carrying out assessments of family support for elderly people with chronic diseases so that it can improve the quality of life of elderly people, especially those suffering from chronic diseases. Keywords: cadre empowerment; assessment; support for elderly families; chronic diseases.

tittel: P350 Children discharged directly home from the paediatric intensive care unit
sammendrag: Background The process of discharging a patient directly home from the paediatric intensive care unit is distinctly different from discharging a patient to a hospital ward or another hospital. Whether these differences increase the risk of communication errors or increased mortality has not been previously investigated in a paediatric cohort. For adult populations the discharge of select patients directly home from the intensive care unit is not associated with increased healthcare utilisation or increased mortality. Whether discharge directly home from the Paediatric Intensive Care Unit is associated with increased mortality has not been previously investigated in the literature. Aim To describe cases presenting for admission to the Paediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) but who are sufficiently recovered to be discharged directly home. Methods This single centre retrospective descriptive study was conducted from the 1st July 2012 to 1st July 2018. Data was extracted from the PICU Clinical Information Portfolio system. Patients with a palliative diagnosis were excluded from this study. Results 87 patients were discharged directly home in the 6 year study period. No patients died within 30 days of discharge. The median PIM 3 score was 0.0139 (IQR 0.0072–0.0347). Of patients admitted diagnoses were 41% Respiratory, 33% Peri-operative, 8% Cardiology, 6% Toxicology, 5% Neurology, 5% Gastrointestinal, 2% Allergy and 1% Trauma. 69 (79%) of patients had a past medical history. In 34 (39%) admissions patients had a tracheostomy. There were no discharges against medical advice. The primary team was informed of discharge for 84 (97%) patients. A documented follow-up plan was recorded for 46 (53%) patients. There was written communication with the patients general practitioner for 22 (25%) patients. 5 (6%) patients were discharged outside the hours of 9:00–17:00. Conclusions For the most part primary teams were informed and the majority of patients had follow-up arranged, however communication with the GP was poor. Following the results of this study a standardised template was introduced at our institution to improve the discharge process.

tittel: Relevance to identify patients with uncomplicated presentation at the index hospitalization for suspected acute myocarditis to better plan follow-up
kilde: European Heart Journal Acute Cardiovascular Care
sammendrag: Acute myocarditis (AM), a generally self-resolving inflammation of the myocardium, mainly affects adolescents and young adults with a male prevalence (60–80%).1 The estimated incidence is between 4 and 14 per 100 000 individuals each year with an overall estimated mortality rate between 1 and 7%.1 Nevertheless, most patients have an uneventful course after the initial hospitalization for AM.2,3 A previous retrospective Italian multicentre registry (Lombardy registry) studied 443 patients with AM diagnosed by either endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) or increased troponin plus oedema and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) at cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). At the time of hospital admission, 118 patients (26.6%) had left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) < 50%, sustained ventricular arrhythmias (VAs), or a low cardiac output syndrome, whereas 325 (73.4%) had no such complications (uncomplicated presentation).3 At the 5-year follow-up, excluding the events during the acute phase, major AM-related cardiac events [post-discharge death and heart transplantation (HTx), sustained VA treated with electric shock or ablation, and symptomatic heart failure (HF) needing device implantation] occurred in 2.8% of the overall population, with a higher incidence in patients with complicated forms at baseline presentation (10.8% vs. 0% in uncomplicated AM; log-rank P < 0.0001; Table 1).3 Other studies have identified potential markers of events after the acute phase of AM, including patients with normal or nearly normal LVEF.4,5 In particular, it has been demonstrated that among 374 patients with AM diagnosed by CMR, the evidence of septal inflammatory involvement was associated with future events (sudden cardiac death, VA, and HF hospitalizations).4 Other studies identified, in a small proportion of patients (<5%), the presence of pathogenic or likely pathogenic desmosomal gene variants.5–7 These patients had an increased risk of VA or myocarditis recurrence despite a normal or nearly normal LVEF.5,7 Thus, a proportion of patients with AM initially classified at low risk based on clinical and echocardiographic criteria may have a specific localization of inflammation, detectable at CMR, or a genetic background that put them at higher risk of adverse events at follow-up. Main differences between the current population with uncomplicated acute myocarditis in the Swiss registry and in the previously published Lombardy registry AM, acute myocarditis; CMRI, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging; EMB, endomyocardial biopsy; HTx, heart transplantation; LVEF, left ventricular ejection fraction; Q, quartile; VA, ventricular arrhythmia. aEchocardiogram performed on admission or in emergency department. Main differences between the current population with uncomplicated acute myocarditis in the Swiss registry and in the previously published Lombardy registry AM, acute myocarditis; CMRI, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging; EMB, endomyocardial biopsy; HTx, heart transplantation; LVEF, left ventricular ejection fraction; Q, quartile; VA, ventricular arrhythmia. aEchocardiogram performed on admission or in emergency department. In the current issue of the European Heart Journal – Acute Cardiovascular Care, Schelldorfer et al.8 report the occurrence of cardiac events after AM in a retrospective Swiss registry during a 9-year period (2013–20). The authors identified 1439 patients who were admitted with AM based on ICD-10 administrative data that also included the codes for rheumatic myocarditis (I01.2 and I09.0). The median follow-up was 39 months (∼3.3 years), and the comparator was a matched population undergoing laparoscopic appendectomy hospitalization for the first time. The authors provided retrospectively their own definition of uncomplicated presentation as the absence of cardiac events during index hospitalization in the discharge report. Overall, the rate of diagnostic assessment was low, or simply not reported, as we can presume for transthoracic echocardiography, which was performed only in 20.8% of patients (n = 300). Cardiac magnetic resonance was performed only in 24.9% (n = 360) of patients during hospitalization that had a median duration of 3 days (first to third quartile: 2–5 days). It is likely that CMR was performed after discharge, but the results were not available. In particular, we do not know whether CMR would have led to reclassification of the diagnosis, for instance in patients with myocardial infarction and no obstructive coronary disease (MINOCA).9 Schelldorfer et al. report that 203 (14.1%) patients with uncomplicated AM had a rehospitalization due to cardiovascular events during follow-up with an estimated annual incidence rate of 4.4 per 100 person-years, a figure significantly higher compared with a matched population who underwent laparoscopic appendectomy (hazard ratio of 42.3). This was based on a composite outcome including hospitalization for myocarditis recurrence (6.0%, n = 87), HF (0.8%, n = 11), diagnosis of dilated cardiomyopathy (0.1%, n = 1), VA (0.7%, n = 10), cardiac arrest (0.4%, n = 6), cardiogenic shock (0.3%, n = 4), supraventricular tachycardia (0.3%, n = 4), atrial fibrillation or flutter (0.4%, n = 6), second- or third-degree atrioventricular block (0), sick sinus syndrome (0.1%, n = 1), or pericardial disease including acute pericarditis (8.6%, n = 124), cardiac device implantation (0.3%, n = 4), or HTx (0.1%, n = 1). In addition, it is worth noting that during follow-up, 126 patients (8.8%) were admitted with a diagnosis of ischaemic heart disease, likely due to a previous misdiagnosis of AM. Another surprising and counterintuitive finding is that among uncomplicated AM, the only two independent protective factors for future adverse events were female sex and older age. These two factors have been identified as risk factors for cardiac death or HTx after AM.10,11 It could be possible that the composition of the endpoint that included recurrence of myocarditis and pericardial disease can explain the different association between events and age and sex. Unfortunately, the authors did not have data on potential deaths that could have occurred without hospitalization, and for this reason, they did not provide this piece of information. The investigators should be commended for the collection of administrative data that enrich our knowledge about the risk of rehospitalizations after a suspected AM. The main message that can be derived from this study is that it is fundamental to reach the most accurate diagnosis of AM during the index hospitalization, and CMR should be performed timely even in presumed myocarditis with uncomplicated presentation to avoid misdiagnoses. If we compare the outcomes after AM discharge in the Lombardy registry, there were only 2 patients (0.6%) with hospitalization due to ischaemic heart disease in the follow-up vs. 126 (8.8%) in the Swiss registry (Table 1). It could be possible that patients with AM deserve a longer duration of hospitalization than 3 days to reduce the risk of early rehospitalization due to misdiagnosis or undertreatment of symptoms, especially chest pain derived from myocarditis or pericardial involvement. When the authors blanked the events that occurred within the first month of follow-up, there were an estimated 3.5-fold decrease in the total endpoint events that patients had during follow-up. This estimation was based on the drop in the hazard ratio for the risk of the primary endpoint occurrence from 42.3 to 12.4 excluding the events that occurred in the first month and graphically from the comparison of the Kaplan–Meier failure estimate curves of cardiovascular composite outcome including or excluding the events that occurred during the first month (Figure 1 in the manuscript). In the same direction, the authors reported a significant reduction of events after discharge in patients with immediate cardiac diagnostics vs. those without immediate cardiac diagnostics, 111 events out of 590 patients (18.8%) vs. 93 out of 851 patients (10.9%), with an estimated annual incidence rate of 3.2 per 100 person-years among those with immediate diagnostics vs. 6.3 per 100 person-years among those without immediate diagnostics. We believe that the simple criterion of uncomplicated presentation to identify patients at very low risk of major cardiac events including cardiac death and HTx proposed in the Lombardy registry are still valid among patients with definite diagnosis of AM.1 The main differences between the current Swiss registry and the previous Lombardy registry are presented in Table 1.3,8 Having a persistent LVEF < 50% (even without HF symptoms), a variable not captured by the Swiss registry, at index hospitalization can be a risk factor for future development of HF or VA, and these patients should undergo a stricter follow-up planning and periodic outpatient visits to monitor cardiac function and the risk of VA.12–14 Furthermore, it must be recognized that even among uncomplicated patients with AM, about 4% have an associated autoimmune disorders that could explain a potentially unfavourable outcome in the long term.3 Searching for potential associated autoimmune disorder is thus relevant in patients with first diagnosis of AM.11 Another relevant finding that the Swiss registry has pointed out is the risk of myocarditis recurrence that was observed in 6% in this population, in line with previous observations.3,15 Identification of patients with myocarditis recurrence should steer physician’s attention towards a potential genetic background for pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in desmosomal genes.5,7 The coexistence of a large extent of fibrosis on CMR involving the ventricular septum, a high ventricular arrhythmic burden defined by a high burden of premature ventricular complexes or non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, and a family history of myocarditis beyond myocarditis recurrence can increase the likelihood of a positive genetic testing among patients with AM.5,7 These patients with AM and a genetic background of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy are at risk of developing biventricular or left prevalent cardiomyopathies in the long-term and could explain the excess in VA and resuscitated cardiac death observed in the current registry. As a final message, we believe that this registry can increase our awareness of a hidden subgroup of patients with AM at increased risk of arrhythmic events, even if at first glance they could have been classified as low risk, but the identification of these patients requires that key investigations such as CMR have been obtained since the index hospitalization. No new data were generated or analysed in support of this research.

tittel: Safe or Sorry? Risk Reduction and Humanism in Newborn Medicine
sammendrag: Is my infant safer with a nanny or in day care? Which car seat is the safest choice for our family? New parents are confronted with a barrage of decisions that require them to balance risks and benefits. In the era of coronavirus disease 2019, decision-making regarding risk reduction and safety has been in the limelight more than ever. Some families tolerate risk for potential benefit, whereas others prioritize risk reduction; this is often informed by their personal situation, family history, and cultural and socioeconomic background. Physician recommendations on risk reduction are guided by physiology, training, and practice standards. However, they are also influenced by a myriad other factors, including our own biases, risk tolerance, experience with clinical sentinel events, and social power imbalances.Risk analysis in the newborn period is especially challenging. It requires new parents to face previously unknown situations during a stressful time, as they discover how to care for both themselves and their uniquely vulnerable infant. This article discusses 3 common newborn topics, fever, sleep, and jaundice, and reflects on how medical advice regarding risk during this period can be profoundly impactful. We explore how physicians can compassionately communicate with families regarding risk reduction and improve family-centered medical decision-making.“Doctor, is it okay to have visitors around the infant? Should they wear masks? His big sister is sick, is that okay?” As a doctor, my guidance to these common questions is focused on prevention of admission for fever in a neonate, invasive diagnostics including lumbar puncture, and the rare but potentially catastrophic possibility of bacterial meningitis.As a mother, when I hear these questions, I think of my own family’s efforts to reduce risk of infectious exposure after my daughter was born very early in the pandemic. Before vaccines were available and when maximum precautions were recommended, we chose to limit family to brief visits outdoors in the first month of my daughter’s life. However, attempting to eliminate risk had a humanistic cost. My husband and I were alone on a figurative island with 2 young children, sleep deprived, stressed, and without the support system that had kept us afloat in the past. My children’s grandparents missed out on irreplaceable moments, holding and loving a new infant in its first days of life. We made the best decision we could at the time, and although I am still fairly risk-averse, this experience influences my perspective.Although admission for fever in a neonate is a common event, bacterial meningitis is quite rare,1 and fever in a neonate recommendations have evolved significantly in the last few years.2 How should we share the nuances of this data with families? How can we empower families to join us in consensus-based decision-making that is both within the spectrum of best practices while also incorporating their values?2 The risks of newborn infection should be shared, but also contextualized.I always thought to myself, “You survived residency… you’ll be fine with a newborn.” Famous last words. Pediatricians transition to an interesting place after the birth of our children. Suddenly, a world where you previously guided families as an expert is yours to experience firsthand as a novice.It was the second night of having my first infant home after 10 days in the NICU. By discharge, her umbilical stump had already come off, we had extra practice at diapers and swaddling, and I had an established milk supply and plan for home. I thought we were set. Fast-forward to the out-of-body experience of my husband frantically shaking me at 2 Am saying, “Wake up!” as we realized that I had drifted asleep while breastfeeding in bed. After I had ingrained in him the dangers of cosleeping (also referred to as bed-sharing) and best safe sleep practices3,4 leading up to our daughter’s birth, his face said it all.Although seldom discussed by physician parents, I know I am not alone in my experience with unintentional cosleeping. When rounding on my newborn service now, as a mother of 2, how do I approach a parent who I find cosleeping when I enter the room? I personally have experienced the exhaustion they are feeling; was this an accidental occurrence or an intentional choice, and does that influence my approach? Blanket rejection of cosleeping does not acknowledge the culturally contextualized spectrum of home sleep choices that exists, often despite knowledge of the risks. How do I integrate my personal experience as a fatigued mother waking every few hours into these discussions to protect others from unintentional cosleeping? Is it possible to acknowledge this very personal experience without contradicting my physician knowledge about cosleeping risks? How does safety data affect my guidance for a term, breastfed infant in a nonsmoking household?5“When is your follow-up appointment?” It is discharge day, and the sleepy, early term infant is down 9% and has an elevated bilirubin. The first-time mother really wants to avoid formula as she waits for her milk to arrive. Her follow-up appointment is in 3 days, as the office is closed over the weekend.Jaundice, with tidy risk-stratification and evidence-based numerical thresholds for each hour of life, seems like a straightforward part of newborn rounds. But there is a lot to consider when forming a follow-up plan.6 Is the latch going well enough to avoid supplementation or the complexities of the pump? What home breastfeeding support is available? When should they follow up, and how is that influenced by weather, transportation, and the level of parental experience? Some physicians might delay discharge to repeat laboratories or even initiate a few hours of phototherapy under the prescribed threshold, to avoid a potential readmission. Maybe these bilirubin numbers are not so tidy.I think back to my own devotion to breastfeeding in the first days at home, syringe feeding drops of colostrum to my first infant as I got engorged and nipple blisters worsened. Nine years and 3 infants later, I wish I had been more flexible. I will choose what personal retrospective wisdom I share, and for some patients, introduce data showing that small-volume formula supplementation may actually increase her eventual breastfeeding success and simultaneously improve the infant’s jaundice.7 The recommendations I make to this new mother, standing before me with car seat in hand, must be both clinically sound and sensitive to the emotionally and physically challenging postpartum days ahead. Our medical advice to parents on jaundice, formula, and follow-up must balance the humanistic impact of our recommendations with relative risk.Bogardus et al (1999) describes the 5 dimensions of decision-making about risk.8 The first 4 dimensions, including type, permanence, timing, and probability of risk, are within the physician domain. The fifth, the relative value or importance of the risk to the patient, inherently requires the patient and family perspective and optimal communication.Previous research has identified a cognitive bias toward protocolizing risk-based decisions.9 Although it may be simpler to always require a child with an elevated bilirubin to follow up in 48 hours, excessive dependence on cognitive shortcuts may lead to the exclusion of family preferences and individual circumstances. Protocol-based risk reduction may work well for simple situations, but it performs poorly in nuanced scenarios where risks and benefits must be balanced.9Risk discussions should incorporate both physician experience and family perspective. We should strive to counsel using our scientific knowledge and clinical experience, while acknowledging relative risks and incorporating the family’s perspective. When it is appropriate, we should provide a spectrum of reasonable options for families to consider on the basis of their circumstances and priorities. These steps reflect the ethical principle of autonomy, and although pediatric ethics have their own complexities,10 autonomy should not be overshadowed by the sometimes patriarchal culture of medicine. Prescriptive advice is often warranted and sometimes desired by parents. However, we can let well-informed parents make appropriate decisions for their family. Even the clinical practice guidelines for management of febrile infants recommend incorporating shared decision-making when appropriate.2For optimal medical care tailored to each patient, the “in-between” sometimes must be addressed. Which is riskier, instructing a family on best practices for safe sleep and ignoring signals that they will not be following guidelines, or recognizing their choices and discussing strategies to make safer decisions? Avoiding absolutist language (“you must,” “you cannot”) and brainstorming compromise is likely to support a more honest doctor–patient relationship.11 In an environment of scientific skepticism, our relationship with our patients thrives when we acknowledge and respect parental values and save unilateral recommendations for high-priority topics with well-supported recommendations. It is in these safe conversations that trust is gained and the likelihood of adherence to recommendations is improved.Attempting to eliminate risk for children might seem appealing; however, the pandemic has reminded us that eliminating risk has never been possible and attempting to do so can carry its own costs. Our individual humanistic experiences can help us connect with patient families, better understand what is important to them, and make the difference between what is heard and what is ultimately adopted.

tittel: Neurodevelopmental Follow-Up of a Child With Parechovirus Meningitis: Parental Perspective and Physicians’ Reflection
sammendrag: In this article, we report the case of a now 3.5-year-old boy who was born at 34 6/7 weeks’ gestation. He presented during infancy with fever on postnatal day 10 and was diagnosed with human parechovirus (HPeV) infection. After initial treatment, he was followed in a multidisciplinary clinic and was later found to have global developmental delay. This case highlights key elements of long-term follow-up in infants with HPeV meningitis, presents the parents’ perspective of their journey, and includes our reflections on their experience.The male infant was born to a healthy 34-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman. The first trimester pregnancy screening was unremarkable, and the fetal anatomy ultrasonography was normal. Maternal serologic conditions were protective, and she received routine prenatal medications including iron and prenatal vitamins. Approximately 2 weeks prior to delivery, she experienced a diarrheal gastrointestinal illness lasting 1 week, with similar symptoms in the father and older sibling. The infant was delivered via spontaneous vaginal delivery at 34 6/7 weeks’ gestation following unstoppable preterm labor. His Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. However, he developed respiratory distress and required continuous positive airway pressure. His head circumference was 32 cm (3rd percentile), birth weight was 2560 g (60th percentile), and his length was 45.5 cm (45th percentile). He transitioned to room air after 48 hours and required gavage feedings because of immature oral feeding skills.At 9 days of age, while still in the hospital, the infant developed fever and recurrent apneic episodes. A complete sepsis evaluation including a lumbar puncture was done, and broad-spectrum antibiotics with ampicillin and cefotaxime were initiated at meningitic doses. On the following day, he developed apneic episodes with increasing frequency, requiring intubation. One apneic episode was accompanied by rhythmic tongue thrusting and another episode by eye blinking, and he was treated with one dose of intravenous lorazepam for suspected seizures. He was then transferred to our neonatal neurocritical care unit for further investigations and management.On admission, the infant was subdued but appropriately responsive. He was noted to have hiccups, and an amplitude-integrated electroencephalogram was obtained, which demonstrated seizure activity. He received another dose of lorazepam followed by an intravenous phenobarbital load for repetitive seizure activity. Continuous video-integrated electroencephalogram monitoring was initiated, which showed mild diffuse encephalopathy; however, no further seizure activity was identified over the next 24 hours. Cranial ultrasonography at 13 days of age showed patchy areas of increased periventricular echogenicities in the white matter (Figure 1). Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at 14 days of age revealed extensive diffusion restrictions involving the bilateral supratentorial white matter regions with confluent left occipitotemporal cortex involvement. There was also an associated acute pre-Wallerian degeneration involving the corticospinal tracts, corpus callosum, and bilateral thalami pulvinar (Figure 2). These neuroimaging findings were highly suggestive of a viral infection of the brain. The blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cultures obtained at the outside hospital were negative with CSF analysis showing white blood cell count 0/mm3 to 2/mm3, red blood cell count 65/mm3, protein 0.96 g/L, and glucose 2.6 mmol/L. However, the CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test was positive for HPeV. His urine culture grew Enterococcus fecalis at low colony count, which was not felt to be clinically significant, and his antibiotics were discontinued. He was extubated to room air, received nasogastric tube feedings, and gradually established full oral feeding. His neurological examination before discharge was within normal limits. He was discharged home at 17 days of age with close follow-up planned with neonatal neurology, neurodevelopmental follow-up, infectious diseases, and audiology.The infant was cared for at home by his parents, who demonstrated active engagement in his care and development. He passed the hearing screening test at 4 weeks of age. His pediatrician referred him to ophthalmology at several weeks of age due to concern for atypical movements of the right eye. He had his initial follow-up, a routine check-in conducted via telephone by the neonatal neurodevelopmental follow-up (NNFU) clinic, at 6 weeks of corrected age. The parents did not have any concerns at that time about his growth or development. No seizures were reported in the interim. Further follow-up plan and anticipatory guidance were provided, including recommendations to support early motor and language development, including supervised tummy time and fostering a language-rich environment.At his 4-month corrected age combined neonatal neurology and NNFU clinic visit, he presented with steady growth. The Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination score was within optimal range. He showed good head control, appropriate midline orientation, and symmetric spontaneous movements. His cranial nerves were intact with appropriate visual attention. Muscle bulk and power were normal for age, deep tendon reflexes were slightly brisk (+3), and no clonus was elicited. Axial and appendicular tone were optimal for his age, with no asymmetries. Postural reactions were appropriate for his corrected age. His gross motor skills, assessed by the Alberta Infant Motor Scale, were age appropriate. Socio-adaptive/behavioral and language assessments were also appropriate with conjugated gaze, smiling, and cooing. He was noted to have right esotropia, and there was concern for decreased visual field in the right eye. Further follow-up plan was provided with recommendations for encouraging play skills and fine motor skills by providing a variety of age-appropriate toys and exercises to encourage hands to midline, focusing on communication skills by daily reading and face-to-face time, and fostering gross motor skills by encouraging symmetry and facilitating rolling and supported sitting.At his 8-month and 12-month corrected age NNFU clinic visits, he showed good head control, midline orientation, and symmetric spontaneous movements with smooth antigravity activity. His cranial nerves were appropriate along with his muscle bulk and tone. Deep tendon reflexes were slightly brisk (+3) but symmetric, and no clonus was elicited. Primitive reflexes were appropriately diminished for age. Postural reactions, including lateral tilting and forward protective extension, were appropriate for his corrected age. He was being followed closely by ophthalmology who had recommended intermittent left eye patching and wearing corrective glasses for myopia and astigmatism. He had a mild left-sided plagiocephaly, and a decrease in his weight was noted (17th percentile) on the 12-month visit. He continued to make progress in his neurodevelopment, showing age-appropriate development in gross motor, fine motor, speech/language and communication, and social-emotional domains. His parents were provided with anticipatory guidance together with information pamphlets about age-appropriate motor, play, and speech and language activities over the next several months.At his 18-month corrected age visit to the NNFU clinic, his parents shared their concerns that he was not walking. His neurological examination remained normal. He demonstrated stable head and trunk control and smooth and coordinated movements. His cranial nerves were intact, and he had normal axial and appendicular tone without asymmetries. His deep tendon reflexes were +3 and symmetric, with no clonus. He was also assessed using the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, 4th Edition, to objectively assess cognitive, language, and motor functioning. He received a cognitive composite score of 54 (<1st percentile), a language composite score of 75 (5th percentile), and a motor composite score of 72 (3rd percentile), with scaled scores of 4 (2nd percentile) for receptive language, 7 (16th percentile) for expressive language, 6 (9th percentile) for fine motor, and 4 (2nd percentile) for gross motor skills (all based on corrected age). With these scores, his development across all domains fell below age expectations, with expressive language and fine motor skills relatively stronger than receptive language and gross motor skills. Cognitively, he demonstrated emerging problem-solving abilities such as searching for missing objects, ringing a bell, and removing a Cheerio from a bottle, though relational play was not observed. Language assessment revealed limited receptive skills. He responded to his name and some familiar objects but did not yet identify body parts or clothing items, and expressive language skills included vocalizations, gestures, and a few word approximations, with approximately 10 words reported at home. Motor evaluation showed fine motor progress, including palmar grasp and isolated index finger use, but he was unable to stack blocks. Gross motor skills included reciprocal crawling, pulling to stand, and cruising, though he required support to stand and was not yet walking independently. Overall, he presented with global developmental delays, requiring continued monitoring and early intervention. Referrals for occupational therapy, physiotherapy, and speech and language pathology services were placed, along with recommendations for home activities to improve motor development and speech and language skills.At his 3-year visit to the NNFU clinic, he continued to demonstrate delays across multiple areas of development; however, his parents were pleased with his developmental progress. His parents completed the Ages & Stages Questionnaire–3, which indicated areas of concern in communication, problem-solving, and personal-social skills, with gross and fine motor domains requiring monitoring. At this visit, his head circumference was 45.9 cm (<1st percentile), length 88.4 cm (2nd percentile), and weight 12.4 kg (11th percentile). His neurological examination remained normal with appropriate head and neck control and normal gait, cranial nerves, and tone. His deep tendon reflexes were +3 and symmetric, with no clonus. His Bayley 4th edition scores showed a cognitive composite of 54 (<1st percentile) and a language composite of 65 (1st percentile). He was walking independently, using both hands with a pincer grasp, and communicating with mostly 2-word sentences. He was also socially interactive. His parents reported occasional biting when frustrated. He was wearing glasses. He was attending a center-based daycare full-time and was well-supported by community services, including speech and language pathology and occupational therapy, low-vision services, a social worker, and an integration resource worker. A diagnosis of global developmental delay was provided, and a follow-up clinic visit was scheduled with the neuropsychology clinic at school age.Below are the questions we asked his parents about their journey during his initial hospital course and after discharge. The child was 3.5 years old at the time the parents provided these responses, which are presented verbatim.“The most challenging part was navigating the sleeping arrangements during our stay. We slept on floors, chairs, and pull-out couches for several days because access to the Ronald McDonald House [family accommodation center] was delayed—we had arrived on a Friday night, and the staff member needed to complete the referral did not work weekends. We also didn’t learn until days later that there was a parent McDonald lounge and shower facilities available within the hospital.“Beyond the physical discomfort, we struggled with anxiety and uncertainty about the future, as there was so much information coming from different departments. We didn’t always understand who was responsible for what, and what the test results actually meant. The emotional burden of being separated from our other child was extremely difficult, compounded by the physical strain of being postpartum and managing breastfeeding and pumping around the clock. That said, I must mention how wonderful the lactation room was; it provided a clean, calm, and supportive space and the setup for storing breast milk in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) was truly excellent. Despite all of this, the NICU nurses and team were wonderful, always kind, compassionate, and supportive. I just wish we had known about the available services earlier or that some of these supports could have been proactively put in place on our behalf, considering the emotional state we were in.”“Having a dedicated parent liaison or social worker available over weekends to help coordinate accommodations and provide information about available support would have made a huge difference. A brief orientation or welcome package explaining facilities (like showers, lounges, and available resources) would also have helped us settle in more quickly. Emotional support services, such as counseling or peer support for parents, would have been especially valuable in managing the stress and uncertainty of those first few days.”“He is a loving, easygoing little boy who brings joy to everyone around him. He learns quickly but benefits from a more one-on-one approach. He adores music, dancing, and singing, truly the life of the party, and loves giving hugs and cuddles. He’s incredibly active and happiest when biking or playing with anything that has wheels. He’s also thriving in gymnastics, which we started after noticing his natural love for tumbling and jumping. He recently began skating and is about to start swimming lessons. With time and gentle guidance, he adapts well to group settings and has been making great progress overall.”“He continues to experience some visual challenges, which we’re still working to fully understand. This likely explains why he needs one-on-one assistance throughout the day; he learns best when activities are adapted so he can clearly see and understand what’s happening. Despite these challenges, we feel incredibly fortunate; his recovery and development have been above expectations, and he continues to amaze us with his resilience and curiosity. We discovered many helpful resources once he started daycare, but we’re not familiar with what supports exist within the school system and that uncertainty adds to our worries as we navigate this next stage. I wish we knew more, possibly through peer support groups of parents who have gone through a similar experience.”“Advocate for your child; always trust your instincts. If you notice anything unusual, even if it seems minor, speak up. Build a strong team of professionals to support your child’s development and never decline services offered to you. If appointments start to feel overwhelming, communicate that early; many care teams can coordinate or combine appointments to reduce the strain on your schedule. Keep a binder of all medical reports, assessments, and recommendations; it makes it much easier to track progress and share information between professionals. Above all, be patient with yourself and your child, progress takes time, and every small step is worth celebrating.”These parental insights provide valuable context for understanding the broader impact of neonatal illness on families and set the stage for our own reflections on how such experiences can guide improvements in care.Reading the words of his parents was humbling. They describe their NICU experiences that we often do not see in the rush of clinical care, such as sleeping on floors, not knowing where to shower, unclear roles, and trying to absorb complex information while worrying about another child at home. These are issues we could have anticipated and addressed better. Although our NICU has a structured parent orientation and family support framework, this family’s experience highlights the challenges that can arise when access to these resources is delayed early in admission, particularly over weekends. A simple orientation, earlier involvement of social work on weekends, and clearer guidance about available supports would have eased a lot of their stress. We are glad they felt supported by the clinical team, but their experience shows that kindness alone is not enough. Families need predictable systems and proactive communication, especially in the first days when everything feels chaotic.Their child’s progress is wonderful to read about and speaks to their dedication. Their concerns about his vision, learning needs, and navigating school also make it clear that our responsibility does not stop at discharge. We need to be connecting families with community and peer resources early. Their honesty is invaluable, highlighting exactly where improvements are needed and reminding us that the NICU journey is shaped as much by the environment and communication as by medical care. Their insights also point to clear system-level gaps we can address, such as structured orientation checklists, ensuring weekend social work coverage, and strengthening communication pathways for families during the early overwhelming days of hospitalization.
